young.html: James Joyce was an Irish writer. His first novel follows a boy named Stephen Dedalus as he grows up in Dublin, from a little child to a young man who decides to become a writer.

The book starts the way a small child hears the world, with a bedtime story about a "moocow" and the smells and songs of home. Then Stephen goes away to boarding school. He is small and shy, and he wonders about big questions. In his geography book he writes his name and his address, going all the way out to the universe.

young.name: gb-joyce-stairs
young.cap: Climb the five chapters of Stephen's growing up.

young.html: For parents: the later chapters, about Stephen as a teenager, include a long, frightening sermon about hell and his private struggles. They are for older readers; chapter 1 is a fine read-aloud with explanation.

Your address in the universe. Like Stephen, write your name, then your house or street, town, state or county, country, continent, "The World" and "The Universe," each on its own line. Then wonder, as Stephen did: what comes after the universe?

full.html: James Joyce (1882–1941) was born in Dublin, educated by Jesuits at Clongowes Wood College, Belvedere College and University College Dublin, and left Ireland in 1904 to live in Trieste, Zurich and Paris. A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man appeared as a serial in 1914–15 and as a book in New York in 1916. It draws closely on his own youth. His later novels, Ulysses (1922) and Finnegans Wake (1939), are among the most daring of the century.
The style grows with Stephen. The novel opens in a small child's language:

full.text: Once upon a time and a very good time it was there was a moocow coming down along the road and this moocow that was coming down along the road met a nicens little boy named baby tuckoo....

full.html: By the last chapter, Stephen is a university student arguing about beauty in long, precise sentences, and the book ends in pages from his own diary.

full.name: gb-joyce-stairs
full.cap: Each chapter ends in a moment of triumph that the next chapter tests. Our summary.

full.html: Stephen is caught between three powers that want his loyalty: his family, the Catholic Church in which he was raised, and Irish nationalism. In chapter 3 a preacher's sermon on hell terrifies him into confession and a period of intense devotion. In chapter 4 he is invited to consider the priesthood, and turns it down. Walking on the beach, he sees a girl wading in the sea and feels a burst of joy that he takes as his call to art. In chapter 5 he resolves to leave Ireland and to make his life as a writer, using, as he says, "silence, exile, and cunning."
Joyce's word for the sudden insights that end many scenes was "epiphany": a moment when an ordinary thing shows its meaning. The Portrait is built from such moments.

The name Dedalus points to Daedalus, the craftsman of Greek myth who made wings to escape from a labyrinth. Stephen hopes to fly free from the nets of family, faith and nation, but the myth also recalls Icarus, who flew too high.
Taking Stephen as Joyce's perfect hero. Joyce often smiles at Stephen's pride; the title says "a young man," and later books show him older and less sure.

items: Augustine's Confessions, earlier on this ladder, is the first great story of a young man's inner struggle with faith; Joyce's book is a modern counterpart that turns the other way.
Aquinas, also on this ladder, supplies Stephen's theory of beauty (wholeness, harmony and radiance), as Stephen reads him.
Ovid's Metamorphoses gave Joyce his epigraph and the myth of Daedalus.
Woolf and others, later in this era, took up the method of following a mind from within.
What do we owe our family, our faith and our country? Can we choose our own way and still honor them?
Why does Stephen think he must leave home to become an artist?
What is an "epiphany"? Have you had one?
How does a writer show a child growing up just through the way the sentences change?

questions: Stephen writes his address out to "The Universe." What does that tell you about him?
Stephen was punished unfairly at school and went to the rector to complain. Was that brave?
Why do you think Stephen chose art over the priesthood?
What things in your life pull on your loyalty, as family, faith and country pulled on Stephen?
Is it possible to love a place and still need to leave it?
care: The later chapters include a long sermon describing hell and a teenager's private struggles, told without explicit detail; for older readers. Chapter 1 suits younger readers with an adult.
